questions.q: What is GRANT's basic syntax pattern?
options: GRANT <privilege> ON <object> TO <principal> — like a user, service principal, or group
GRANT <table> TO <schema>
GRANT <user> ON <privilege>
GRANT only works without specifying any object at all
questions.explain: SELECT means read access; MODIFY covers INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE together.

questions.q: Under access control, what role do USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA play, beyond the session convenience from Lesson 39?
options: They become required privileges — a user needs both, plus SELECT on the specific table, before access actually works
They have no additional role under access control
They replace the need for any SELECT grant entirely
They only matter for external tables, not managed ones
questions.explain: All three grants are necessary; any one missing means access still fails, even with a SELECT grant present.

questions.q: What does GRANT SELECT ON SCHEMA nyc_taxi.silver TO `contractors` actually grant?
options: SELECT on every current AND future table in that schema, due to privilege inheritance
SELECT on only the tables that exist in the schema at the moment of the grant
Only USE SCHEMA, not actual SELECT access
Nothing, since GRANT cannot target a schema, only a table
questions.explain: This includes tables created after the grant — a real, easy-to-miss risk of broad grants.

questions.q: Why might granting SELECT at the table level, one table at a time, be preferred over a schema-level grant?
options: It's more work, but far more precise about exactly what's actually being shared, avoiding accidental exposure of future tables
Table-level grants are always faster to execute
Schema-level grants aren't supported by Unity Catalog at all
There's no real difference in precision between the two approaches
questions.explain: Granting broadly is convenient, but it's a real way to accidentally expose more than intended.

options: Undoes exactly what a matching GRANT gave
Permanently deletes the table the privilege was granted on
Only works on catalog-level grants, never table-level ones
Grants a new privilege to a different principal
questions.explain: This is the direct inverse operation, closing off access that was previously opened.
